articles.title: A Chicago couple began protecting their Illinois woodland in the 1980s rather than develop it; decades later, all 126 acres have been bought for a new public preserve carrying their family name
articles.summary: In the 1980s, Dr.
articles.body: In the 1980s, Dr. Shin Theke Kang and his wife, Tae Sue Kang, made a long-term decision to protect a piece of land in southwestern Will County, Illinois, rather than develop it. Over the decades, the Chicago couple restored former agricultural areas, planted thousands of trees and cared for the woodland along Horse Creek. Now, all 126 acres have been acquired by the Forest Preserve District of Will County and will become Horse Creek Preserve, Kang Woodland. The announcement, reported by WJOL, marks the transition of a privately protected landscape into a public natural area. The property contains more than 32,000 surviving trees, including black walnut, oak, maple, ash, pine and cherry, as well as a historic bur oak believed to be hundreds of years old. The new preserve will carry the family name as a lasting tribute to their conservation efforts.A different decision in the 1980sWhen Dr. Shin Theke Kang and Tae Sue Kang acquired the Illinois property, they could have viewed it as land for future development or agricultural use. Instead, they chose to preserve it.The couple began protecting the property in the 1980s, when much of the surrounding landscape was still shaped by farming and other human activity. Their decision was not a short-term project. It became a decades-long effort to care for the land and improve its natural character.Some portions of the property had previously been used for agriculture. The Kangs began reforesting those areas so they could complement the older trees that had remained along Horse Creek.That approach required patience. Newly planted trees need years to become established, and not every sapling survives. The couple continued the work even though the full ecological benefits would not be visible immediately.Today, the result is a mature landscape that contains woodland, open areas and a creek corridor. What began as a private conservation decision has now become the foundation of a public forest preserve.Planting thousands of treesThe Kangs hired a company to plant approximately 40,000 trees across the property. Many survived without irrigation, according to the Forest Preserve District and local reports.The surviving trees include black walnut, oak, maple, ash, pine and cherry. Together, they form a varied woodland rather than a single-species plantation.A diverse tree community can provide different types of habitat throughout the year. Some trees produce nuts or fruit, while others offer nesting spaces, shade and shelter. A mixture of species can also make the woodland more resilient to disease, pests and changing weather conditions.The planted trees now stand alongside legacy trees that were already growing near Horse Creek. That combination gives the property both young and mature habitat.Reforestation also changes the physical character of the land. Tree roots help stabilise soil, fallen leaves return nutrients to the ground and branches create cover for birds, mammals and insects.The Kangs’ work therefore involved more than adding trees to an open field. It helped rebuild a functioning woodland ecosystem over many decades.The ancient bur oakOne of the property’s most notable natural features is a large bur oak that is thought to be hundreds of years old.The tree had been growing along Horse Creek before the Kangs began their restoration work. It represents a link to the landscape that existed before much of the surrounding land was cleared or cultivated.Bur oaks are particularly important in the Midwest. Their thick branches, rugged bark and large acorns provide shelter and food for wildlife. Older trees can also contain cavities and deadwood that support birds, bats, insects and other organisms.A tree that has survived for centuries can serve as a living record of the region’s environmental history. It has endured changes in land use, storms, droughts and generations of human activity.The newly planted trees may eventually reach a similar age, but the bur oak gives the preserve an immediate sense of deep time. It is one of the natural landmarks that makes the property more than a recently created woodland.A preserve along Horse CreekThe new preserve is located in Custer Township in the southwestern part of Will County. The property follows Horse Creek, which flows into the Kankakee River near the Wauponsee Trail.Creek corridors are valuable because they connect different parts of a landscape. Waterways provide drinking and breeding areas, support vegetation and offer routes for wildlife to move between habitats.Trees along streams can shade the water, reduce erosion and help maintain cooler conditions for aquatic organisms. Fallen leaves and branches also contribute organic material to the creek and surrounding soil.The connection to the Kankakee River places the property within a wider watershed. Actions on the land can influence water quality downstream, making forest protection important beyond the boundaries of the preserve itself.The creek also adds a distinctive feature for future visitors. People may experience the preserve not only as a woodland but as a landscape shaped by flowing water, changing seasons and the relationship between forest and stream.From private land to public preserveOn September 9, 2026, the Forest Preserve District of Will County purchased the 126 acres. The property will be known as Horse Creek Preserve, Kang Woodland.The acquisition means that the land will no longer depend solely on private ownership for its protection. The district will manage it as part of the county’s public forest preserve system.That transition can create new opportunities for residents. Public preserves may offer trails, nature observation, educational programs, volunteer activities and other forms of access, depending on the property’s development and management plans.The preserve will not necessarily be opened all at once. Staff may need to assess the land, identify sensitive habitats, plan access routes and determine how to protect the creek and mature trees.A careful opening process can help balance public enjoyment with ecological protection. Natural areas can be damaged by unmanaged foot traffic, invasive species, litter and disturbance during breeding seasons.The district’s responsibility will be to make the woodland available while preserving the conditions that make it valuable.The family name will remainNaming the preserve Kang Woodland creates a permanent connection between the family and the property.Many conservation stories focus on public agencies or large organisations, but the early work here was carried out by two private landowners. The Kangs protected the property long before it became part of the county preserve system.Their name will remind visitors that the woodland exists because someone made a decision decades earlier to preserve and restore it.The name also recognises the difference that individual landowners can make. A single property may appear small compared with a county or regional landscape, but it can provide a vital piece of habitat and create a link between other protected areas.By carrying the Kang name, the preserve will tell its history as people walk through the trees. The land will be public, but its conservation legacy will remain personal.Why private conservation mattersA large amount of wildlife habitat exists on privately owned land. Owners decide whether to develop, farm, restore or protect their property.Private conservation can fill gaps in public land networks. A property may contain a wetland, forest or creek corridor that connects two larger natural areas. Protecting it can help animals move through the landscape and reduce habitat fragmentation.The Kangs’ project also demonstrates the value of long-term ownership. Because they maintained the property over several decades, they were able to see the effects of restoration and preserve features that might otherwise have been lost.Their decision did not rely on an immediate financial return. The benefits developed gradually through tree growth, habitat formation and improved ecological connections.When the public acquisition finally occurred, the Forest Preserve District received more than undeveloped acreage. It acquired a landscape that had already been cared for and shaped by conservation.A living woodland, not just open spaceThe 126 acres will provide more than scenic views.The forest can support songbirds, woodpeckers, mammals, reptiles, amphibians and insects. Different tree ages create different nesting and shelter opportunities, while fallen logs and leaf litter provide habitat near the ground.The creek and its edges may support aquatic organisms, waterfowl and animals that depend on wet environments. Open areas can provide space for wildflowers and pollinators.A healthy woodland also contributes to broader environmental functions. Trees absorb carbon dioxide, release oxygen, reduce erosion and help slow stormwater. Their roots improve soil structure, while their canopies moderate temperatures.These benefits become more valuable as surrounding land is developed. A protected woodland can serve as a refuge for species that lose habitat elsewhere.The preserve may also provide educational value. Students, families and local residents can observe seasonal changes, learn about native trees and see how restoration develops over time.Planning the public futureThe Forest Preserve District purchased the property under its 2025 to 2030 capital improvement program, which includes funding for new land acquisitions. A local report said the district paid approximately $1.3 million for the property.The purchase is the first step in creating the public preserve. Future work may include surveys, trail planning, signage, habitat management and the removal of invasive plants.Any public access plan will need to account for the property’s ecological sensitivity. Horse Creek, mature trees and newly established woodland all require protection.Staff may also monitor how visitors use the property after it opens. If certain areas become heavily disturbed, the district could adjust routes or limit access during particular seasons.The goal is to make the preserve welcoming without treating it like an ordinary park. Its primary purpose is to protect natural resources, while recreation and education can be designed around that mission.A conservation legacy that took decadesThe story of Kang Woodland is a reminder that environmental restoration rarely happens quickly.The Kangs began protecting the property in the 1980s. They planted tens of thousands of trees, restored former agricultural land and preserved older woodland along Horse Creek. Decades later, the land has become a 126-acre public preserve.The timeline matters. A tree planted in the 1980s is now large enough to contribute meaningfully to the forest. A decision that once affected only one family’s property now benefits an entire community.The preserve also shows how private action and public conservation can work together. The Kangs protected and restored the land, while the Forest Preserve District secured its future and created the possibility of public access.Horse Creek Preserve, Kang Woodland, will stand as both a natural area and a record of long-term stewardship. Its trees carry the evidence of years of care, and its name will honour the couple who chose preservation when development might have seemed easier.What began as a private woodland in Illinois has now become a public inheritance for future generations.You use AI every day. articles.title: Studland seahorse habitats 'healing' thanks to eco moorings
articles.summary: Scars in Studland Bay's seagrass meadows, caused by boat anchor chains, are healing, a study finds.
articles.body:
Scars caused to rare seahorse habitats by boat anchors off the Dorset coast are starting to heal, thanks to the installation of new moorings.

In 2021, Studland Bay Marine Partnership began installing the first of dozens of eco-moorings in a bid to reverse damage to delicate seagrass meadows.

A new scientific study has now provided the first evidence that eco-moorings can help restore seagrass, with some scars shrinking by more than 90% over four years.

David Brown, chair of the partnership steering group, called the results "incredibly exciting", adding: "The impact has been beyond our expectations."

Seagrass habitats store carbon, support biodiversity and help protect coastlines from erosion, but are declining globally due to pollution, development, disturbance and climate change .

The research, conducted by Kira Dunn as part of her MSc in Marine Biology with Oceanography at the University of Southampton, analysed monitoring data collected since the first eco-moorings were installed.

Using sonar surveys, historical satellite imagery and five years of monitoring data, the study tracked recovery across 39 damaged areas of seabed.

In the area where 10 trial eco-moorings were installed in 2021, the size of bare patches in the seagrass decreased by an average of 93.6% between 2021 and 2025, shrinking by around 57 sq m each year.

In a second study area, where traditional chain moorings remained until 2023, the scars reduced by 65.4%, around 15.9 sq m a year.

Studland Bay has been a designated a Marine Conservation Zone since 2019 and is home to one of the UK's largest seagrass meadows, supporting species such as the protected spiny seahorse and short-snouted seahorse.

The bay also became a voluntary no-anchor zone in 2021.

Dunn, who graduated this year, said the research project had been "rewarding and positive".

She said: "It's incredibly encouraging to see how quickly this important habitat can regenerate when given the opportunity."

Dr Ken Collins, of the University of Southampton, who supervised the study, said: "Studland Bay is becoming a powerful example of how practical conservation measures can reverse habitat damage and deliver measurable environmental improvements."

Brown, who is also lead ecologist for the National Trust, said: "These results are incredibly exciting, and a huge encouragement to all the organisations and individuals who have given so much time and support to the partnership.

"The impact has been beyond our expectations, and thanks to robust monitoring and research, we have the science to prove how the eco-moorings benefit seagrass and all the species that rely on it."

Studland Bay Marine Partnership is made up of conservation charities, boating organisations, academics, statutory bodies, community groups and businesses, with the aim of restoring Studland's seagrass.

Partners include Dorset Wildlife Trust, Natural England, the National Trust, the Seahorse Trust and the University of Southampton.

articles.title: Bristol venues strike back against AI generated artwork
articles.summary: Café Kino is the latest venue to ban the use of AI artwork over ethical and sustainability concerns.
articles.body:
Communities in the West of England are taking a stance against the use of AI-generated artwork.

Café Kino, based in Stokes Croft, Bristol, has become the latest venue to ban AI-generated posters, while the University of Bristol Students' Union has banned AI artwork at its Freshers Week poster sale.

Bristol-based live music venue Zed Alley also banned AI artwork on its social media channels last month, citing ethical concerns and a lack of originality.

"It fundamentally is terrible for the environment, and it takes the work out of the hands of graphic designers," said Chris Illingworth, who manages the venue's social media platforms.

Illingworth said the venue had received an "overwhelmingly positive" response from customers.

As well as ethical concerns, Zed Alley decided to ban AI-generated posters because of their poor performance on social media.

"I think it's partly that it's missing a human touch and by and large, they look very samey," said Illingworth.

Earlier this week, a mural based on AI-generated artwork was removed from the Jolly Colliers pub in Bedminster after members of the community described it as "disrespectful".

A spokesperson for Punch Pubs & Co, which owns the pub, previously said the mural was a "temporary solution" and that they would work with artists to replace it soon.

Bristol artist Jenny Harrison described the situation as "equal parts funny and tragic", due to the mural's location around the corner from Upfest, Europe's largest street art festival.

Harrison said she had noticed a rise in AI-generated posters.

"It's one of those things where I understand that often budget is a big issue for venues, but again, I think it's such a shame when creatives don't support other creatives."

Generative AI learns from vast quantities of material from the internet, which can be used to generate new content.

This visual material can include images and videos, meaning that an artist's published work can be used to train AI models.

"It makes me feel quite uncomfortable," said Harrison.

"When it comes to AI replacing human creativity, that makes me really worried because creativity is such a purely human trait."

Zase, a Bristol-based graffiti artist, said he did not mind people using AI generated artwork.

"I'm not bothered about what somebody else is doing," he said.

"AI threatens loads of many jobs, graphic designers, office jobs, it is what it is."

Ruby Saunders, a 21-year-old mathematics student at the University of Bristol, said she is often put off by companies using AI artwork.

"It makes me think that they only value money, like profit over the people," she said.

"Because if they got in an actual artist, it means they care about the artist having a living."

After purchasing a poster at the Students' Union's annual poster sale, which she later realised had been designed using AI, Saunders led a motion to ban AI-generated artwork at the event.

"I felt quite upset that I put my money into something that didn't turn out to be what I thought it was," said Saunders, who is against AI artwork due to ethical and environmental concerns.

"It's just using stolen art, and artists aren't getting credited, so they're not getting the money that they should be.

"As well as that, a lot of people accuse artists of [using] AI when it's actually their own work.

"They have to put in a lot more time and effort to show, 'actually, this isn't AI art'."

Saunders said AI's environmental impact was also a major factor.

"Especially with the recent drought, there's a lot of water usage in AI in general, because they need a lot of water for coolant systems," she said.

"A lot of energy is made using crude oil and non-renewable sources. And as well as that, it produces greenhouse gases. It warms up the whole world."

A Bristol SU spokesperson said: "We are very happy to see our students using our democratic mechanism to bring change to the SU and to the University.

"This motion to ban AI, Stolen and Unethical Art at SU Poster Sale was brought forward and passed at Student Council in term 1 of the 2025/26 academic year.

"We did not run a poster sale this Welcome Week."

articles.title: Longleat library first edition reveals Austen's early fans
articles.summary: Several first editions were bought by the 2nd Marquess of Bath during the author's lifetime.
articles.body:
A first edition of Jane Austen's debut novel has shed light on the author's connection with one of Britain's historic country houses.

The 1811 first edition of Sense and Sensibility is on the shelves at Longleat House in Wiltshire, with its title page still carrying the anonymous attribution "By A Lady".

It is thought to have been acquired by the 2nd Marquess of Bath around the time of its publication which historians say is evidence Austen was being read by the elite social class during her lifetime.

Dr James Ford, curator of Longleat House, said the estate had "a wonderful group of early Jane Austen editions", including Emma and Pride and Prejudice.

Sense and Sensibility follows the Dashwood sisters after their father's death leaves the family facing financial uncertainty. It follows the very different ways two young women navigate love, loss and society.

Vandals target ancient stones in 'heritage crime'

Bound in green and brown leather with a gold title, the relatively unassuming volume is among thousands of books in the seven historic libraries at Longleat House.

It is presumed Jane Austen signed her first novel "By a Lady" to maintain her anonymity.

Writing novels for money or public fame was generally considered unfeminine and improper for women of the gentry class during the 18th and 19th centuries.

Her identity as the author only became widely known after Austen's death in 1817, when her brother Henry identified his sister in a biographical notice.

The libraries at Longleat House contain a total collection of around 44,000 historic books, including first editions of Emma and a second edition of Pride and Prejudice.

The edition is evidence that during her lifetime, Austen's books were being read and collected by the elite social class - the very social circle she depicted in her novels.

"An invoice we discovered last year records the 2nd Marquess purchasing Mansfield Park shortly after it was published in May 1814," Ford said.

"He was also one of the first owners of Longleat to open his park gates and hall door to early tourists, rather like the country house visit Austen evokes when Elizabeth Bennet arrives at Pemberley in Pride and Prejudice."

The historic libraries and rare book collections at Longleat can be visited as part of its Libraries VIP Tour.

articles.title: A California homeowner was checking the crawl space beneath his house and discovered the remains of a 29-year-old woman killed in 2006; years later, police arrested her ex-husband
articles.summary: A California homeowner checking the crawl space beneath his house made a disturbing discovery in October 2020 when authorities found unidentified human
articles.body: A California homeowner checking the crawl space beneath his house made a disturbing discovery in October 2020 when authorities found unidentified human remains hidden beneath the property in Big Bear Lake. An autopsy determined that the person had died in a homicide, but investigators initially could not establish the victim’s identity despite DNA testing and other investigative efforts. The case remained unsolved for years until the San Bernardino County Sheriff’s Cold Case Homicide Team took it up in 2023 and submitted the remains for additional DNA analysis. The testing ultimately identified the victim as Jill Maiorca, a 29-year-old woman who had been reported missing from Big Bear Lake in 2007. Investigators later identified her former husband, Jeff Maiorca, as a suspect and arrested him in September 2026.California homeowner discovered human remains beneath Big Bear homeThe investigation began on October 28, 2020, when deputies from the Big Bear Sheriff’s Station responded to a call about a suspicious discovery in the crawl space of a residence in the 39000 block of Forest Road in Big Bear Lake. Deputies and personnel from the Big Bear Fire Department found human remains beneath the residence and recovered them from the crawl space. An autopsy determined that the manner of death was homicide. However, investigators were initially unable to determine who the victim was. DNA testing and other investigative efforts failed to establish the person’s identity, leaving detectives with an unidentified homicide victim and no clear connection to a missing-person case. Authorities later determined that the remains had been concealed beneath the residence without the homeowner’s knowledge. Investigators have not publicly explained how or when the remains were placed there.Cold case team revisits unidentified remainsThe case received a new investigative push in 2023, when the San Bernardino County Sheriff’s Cold Case Homicide Team assumed the investigation. Detectives submitted the remains for additional investigative DNA analysis in an effort to establish the victim’s identity. The additional analysis eventually produced a breakthrough. Investigators identified the remains as those of Jill Maiorca, who had been reported missing from Big Bear Lake in 2007. She was 29 years old. According to the Sheriff’s Department, evidence developed during the renewed investigation indicated that Maiorca was murdered in November 2006, approximately a year before she was reported missing. Her remains had remained unidentified for years after being discovered beneath the Forest Road residence.Jill Maiorca had been missing since 2007Maiorca’s disappearance had been recorded as a missing-person case in Big Bear Lake in 2007. Her eventual identification gave investigators a name to work with and allowed them to examine her history, relationships and circumstances surrounding her disappearance. Los Angeles County court records show that Jeff Maiorca had filed for divorce from Jill in 2004. The divorce case involved minor children, according to records cited by SFGATE. Authorities have not publicly disclosed a possible motive for Jill’s killing. They also have not detailed all the evidence that led investigators to focus on her former husband. The Sheriff’s Department has said the investigation remains ongoing.Former husband arrested nearly 20 years laterAfter the renewed investigation and identification of Jill’s remains, detectives identified her former husband, Jeff Maiorca, as a suspect in her murder. Maiorca, now 53, was arrested on September 21, 2026, according to the San Bernardino County Sheriff’s Department. Maiorca was taken into custody without incident on September 21 and booked into Big Bear Jail on suspicion of murder, according to the San Bernardino County Sheriff’s Department. The Los Angeles Times, citing incarceration records, reported that he was being held in a San Bernardino County jail without bail. SFGATE reported that Maiorca was detained at the Big Bear Lake branch library on Garstin Drive and that his arrest record listed a murder charge. Maiorca has been accused of killing Jill, but the allegations have not been adjudicated in court. Authorities have not said publicly what evidence specifically connected him to the killing or how they believe her remains came to be concealed beneath the home.Court hearing moved to October 12According to ABC7 Los Angeles, Maiorca was initially scheduled for an arraignment on September 23, but the hearing was continued to October 12. The outlet reported that he is facing first- and second-degree murder charges, along with an enhancement alleging the use of a deadly weapon.The case remains an active homicide investigation. The Sheriff’s Department has asked anyone with information about Jill Maiorca’s disappearance or death to contact its Homicide Detail. articles.title: Heavy rain and flooding in Bangkok disrupts traffic and prompts evacuations
articles.summary: BANGKOK — Incessant rain hammered several areas of Thailand‘s capital on Saturday, disrupting traffic and forcing hundreds to evacuate, as authorities declared the city a disaster area.
articles.body: BANGKOK — Incessant rain hammered several areas of Thailand‘s capital on Saturday, disrupting traffic and forcing hundreds to evacuate, as authorities declared the city a disaster area. Thailand’s Meteorological Department warned that the deluge, which has been pouring since Thursday afternoon, would continue in most parts of the country through Sunday. Accumulated rainfall in many areas of Bangkok since Thursday exceeded 30 centimeters (11.8 inches), officials said. Floodwaters spread across the city, particularly in the central and eastern parts, blocking roads and stopping traffic. While not all parts of Bangkok were submerged, the city declared all of its 50 districts a flood disaster area to allow authorities to respond rapidly to the crisis. More than 84,000 people in 21 provinces nationwide were affected by flooding as of Saturday, especially in the central region. Authorities sent emergency warning messages through the cellphones, the government said. Hwang Hwan-chung, who flew from South Korea and has visited Bangkok a dozen times, said he had never seen such “crazy” weather, adding that he couldn’t find a taxi. Sukanya Tongsuk, a resident, said the current flooding was similar to the last time Bangkok was hit in 2011. Meanwhile, Dutch resident Bjorn Franken, who has lived in the capital for two years, said he was able to cope although one event he wanted to attend had been canceled. Many businesses in Bangkok closed on Saturday due to flooding. Cars crawled along waterlogged roads in parts of Bangkok, and bikers were seen pushing their motorcycles. Authorities said some regional bus services from Bangkok to the eastern provinces were suspended. Phetchaburi Road, one of the capital’s busiest, was unusually quiet as vehicles were turned back by floods. Some were left partially submerged. Residents made their way through murky waters, carrying fresh water and food. Some were barefoot and others wearing rubber waders while several wrapped plastic bags around their feet to keep dry. Air traffic control authorities confirmed flight operations were normal but some flights might face delays. Bangkok Gov. Chadchart Sittipunt said despite the heavy rain, flooding should recede once the rain subsides, as city officials work to drain floodwaters as quickly as possible. More than 200 shelters were set up across the city and about 900 people have moved in, Chadchart said.

articles.title: Iran war squeezes Iraq’s economy as oil revenues fall and prices rise
articles.summary: Disrupted oil exports, costlier imports, and a weaker dinar expose Iraq’s economic dependence on oil, foreign goods.
articles.body:
Iraq is a state heavily dependent on imports, from food and medicines to appliances, as well as raw materials for its industries. Its one big export is oil, but it sits on such a huge supply of the natural resource that revenues from the sale of oil abroad offset the imports and ensured that the country had a positive trade surplus.

Things have changed, however, since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran in late February, and the subsequent end to the free flow of trade through the Strait of Hormuz, through which much of the country’s trade with the rest of the world passed. Now, Iraq’s Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has described the country as “facing extraordinary economic challenges”.

Al-Zaidi said earlier this week that Iraq had lost about $60bn in oil revenues as a result of the war, the result of being, for a period, unable to export about 90 percent of its oil through its usual Gulf routes, which have become central to negotiations between Washington and Tehran, with the latter linking free passage through the strait to an easing of US pressure and the lifting of a blockade on Iranian ports.

That’s a massive blow to Iraq: oil revenues account for more than 90 percent of Iraq’s federal budget.

The disruption to shipping routes has also affected supply chains, increasing transport times and costs for Iraqi businesses and consumers, in addition to reducing imports.

One supermarket owner in Baghdad, Alaa-Eddin Sulaibi, estimated that the percentage of imported goods sold at his store was now 70 percent, down from 90 percent before the war started.

“We have no choice but to sell local products, even if they are not of the same quality as imported ones,” he said.

He added that the price of the imported goods had risen by between 25 and 30 percent.

“The reasons [for the price increase] extend beyond disruptions in the Gulf, but also longer delivery times for goods arriving from China, and higher fuel and transportation costs, particularly for trade with Turkiye,” he said.

Several merchants who spoke to Al Jazeera said goods imported from China were now facing significant delays, in some cases taking up to three months to arrive because of the increase in transportation costs as a result of importers being forced to take more circuitous routes to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, or being delayed at the maritime chokepoint.

The crisis has put pressure on the Iraqi dinar, which has dropped against the US dollar, in a development that has triggered concern among Iraqis.

The dollar rose to about 1,600 Iraqi dinars on the parallel market last week, before easing to about 1,575 this week. Prior to the war, it had been about 1,540 Iraqi dinars to the dollar.

The widening gap between the official exchange rate – approximately 1,300 dinars to the dollar – and the parallel market rate has also created uncertainty for businesses and added to the financial burden on consumers. The official market rate is largely not available to everyday people, and the divergence in rates allows for some businesses to obtain dollars at the cheaper official rate, while others are forced to use the parallel market and pay more.

At the same time, the Iraqi government is also dealing with concerns about the availability and transfer of dollars that Baghdad receives through arrangements linked to its oil revenues.

Following the fall of the regime of President Saddam Hussein after the 2003 US invasion of Iraq, the country’s oil revenues were placed in a special account in the US, with money then transferred to Baghdad. This transfer is renewed annually by the US president, with the stated purpose of safeguarding Iraq’s financial resources. But the system also gives Washington a large degree of oversight over the flow of dollars from the account to Iraq.

In April, the Trump administration began halting the shipment of physical cash from the account to Iraq, releasing only electronic dollar transfers, with some reporting indicating that the halt in physical cash transfers was linked to pressure over the activities of Iran-backed militias in Iraq.

Some physical cash shipments resumed in July, but the US has also accused several private Iraqi banks of being involved in large-scale dollar smuggling operations to Iran.

Local reports have suggested that the Central Bank of Iraq (CBI) is facing difficulties supplying commercial banks with sufficient dollars, particularly for financing imports, potentially leading to higher prices in local markets.

The CBI has denied that it is facing a shortage, saying in a statement on Saturday that it “has sufficient foreign reserves to meet all demands for foreign currency”, adding that included “financing foreign trade”.

The central bank blamed the rise in the parallel market dollar exchange rate on “speculation, expectations, and the misuse of regional geopolitical conditions by certain parties seeking to disrupt Iraq’s economic and financial stability”.

The pressure on Iraq’s finances is nevertheless intensifying as the war continues and oil revenues fall.

Mudher Mohammed Salih, the Iraqi prime minister’s financial adviser, said in a television interview this week that the CBI’s foreign reserves had fallen from about $106bn before the war began, to roughly $80bn by late August.

Economists say the crisis has exposed longstanding structural weaknesses in Iraq’s economy, particularly its dependence on oil revenues and imported goods.

“This crisis has revealed the deep imbalances within the structure of the Iraqi economy, most notably the absence of safeguards capable of protecting the economy during times of turmoil,” Ziad al-Hashimi, a PhD researcher in international economics at Anglia Ruskin University, told Al Jazeera.

“The crisis has also shown that the Iraqi government lacks genuine solutions or effective measures that could bring about the kind of structural change needed to overcome the situation,” he added.

Al-Hashimi said that the government’s immediate options were limited.

“All the Iraqi government can do are short-term measures that may have only limited the impact in the coming period, such as resorting to borrowing, which is not a genuine solution,” he said. “Real solutions require a long time before results can be seen. They include diversifying Iraq’s oil export markets abroad, managing public spending in a more systematic way to avoid unnecessary expenditures, and continuing efforts to combat corruption.”

articles.title: In 1958, an Atlanta woman’s wallet slipped behind a theater wall; 65 years later, a renovation uncovered it, giving her family photos and keepsakes they thought were gone forever
articles.summary: In an incredible turn of events, a woman’s wallet, lost in 1958 at Atlanta’s Plaza Theatre, is uncovered during renovations, revealing family photos and keepsakes thought to be lost forever. This remarkable story showcases the power of memories and family connections.
articles.body: Floy Culbreth lost her wallet at Atlanta’s Plaza Theatre in 1958, when she was 40 and raising two children. She never got it back, and it remained hidden inside the theater for 65 years until contractors found it in 2023, while they were renovating the building. They were removing bathroom wall tiles when they uncovered a space that had once been a closet in the manager’s office. Inside were old objects covered in dust and debris, including umbrellas, hats, empty bottles, a weathered shoe box, and an old popcorn display, and Culbreth’s maroon wallet was among them.There were family photographs, raffle tickets, receipts, library and membership cards, and credit cards from Atlanta department stores Rich’s and Davison’s, which were all pieces of her life from 1958. A dentist appointment card also carried a date from that year.The wallet was conveniently hiddenThe theater’s owner was Christopher Escobar, and initially had no idea who the wallet belonged to. Culbreth had died in 2005 at age 87, but her name and the documents inside gave the renovation team enough information to start looking for relatives. Escobar’s wife searched online and found Culbreth’s obituary, which eventually led to the website for the Culbreth Cup, a golf tournament established by Culbreth’s grandsons in her memory. That connected the theater owners with Thea Culbreth Chamberlain, Culbreth’s daughter.Chamberlain was only 6 when her mother lost it at the theater, and when she finally saw it in 2023, she found photographs and other items she had never seen before. The wallet held a library card, PTA membership card, identification cards that belonged to Culbreth’s daughter and two raffle tickets for a Chevrolet giveaway. There were also credit cards from department stores that no longer exist under those names.The wallet had apparently been placed in the theater’s lost-and-found and then forgotten as the building changed hands and its interior was altered. The closet eventually became enclosed behind new construction, which left the wallet sealed inside.The woman behind the walletFloy Culbreth’s family described a woman who stayed closely involved with her Atlanta community for decades after the wallet disappeared. Culbreth was active in her church, volunteered with nonprofit groups and later helped establish the Atlanta chapter of United Cerebral Palsy after a neighbor’s child was diagnosed with cerebral palsy, while also helping establish an early Atlanta day-care centre for children with cerebral palsy.After her daughter had grown up, Culbreth began working as a clerk in the accounting department at Georgia Power in the early 1970s, where she remained for about two decades. Family members remembered her as someone who enjoyed crossword puzzles, pottery, gardening, cooking and movies, particularly films starring Cary Grant and Spencer Tracy.Her daughter also recalled that Culbreth loved books and regularly used her library card, and read everything from romance novels and history books to recipe collections. Those details helped turn the recovered wallet from an old object into a small record of a woman whose life continued for nearly five decades after she left it behind at the theater.The family got it backEscobar cleaned the wallet before returning it to Culbreth’s family, and on Nov. 19, 2023, Chamberlain and other relatives met him at the Plaza Theatre to collect it. Atlanta Journal-Constitution photographs from the reunion show Chamberlain holding the wallet and examining photographs from inside. Some of the pictures showed people the family could no longer identify, which added another layer to the collection of items that had remained untouched since the late 1950s. The wallet had spent decades hidden inside a theater that continued operating around it, and by the time it was found, Culbreth was gone, but the photographs, cards and receipts inside gave her daughter a direct connection to a period of her mother’s life that had otherwise survived only through family memories.You use AI every day. articles.title: Pro-Palestine Action group to rally at Labour conference led by Burnham
articles.summary: Defend Our Juries say Sunday’s action is an ‘integrity test’ for the UK’s new premier.
articles.body:
London, United Kingdom – Protesters are planning to gather in support of Palestine Action at the first Labour Party conference Prime Minister Andy Burnham will preside over.

Sunday’s “mass, silent sign-holding vigil” in Liverpool, close to the conference centre, is in response to the proscription of Palestine Action as a “terrorist” group, said Defend Our Juries, a rights group that organises rallies calling for the government to drop the ban.

Since it was outlawed in July 2025, a civil disobedience campaign has seen more than 3,600 people arrested for showing their support for the group, often while holding signs reading, “I oppose genocide. I support Palestine Action”.

Organisers at Defend Our Juries expect further arrests, saying several hundred people are likely to attend.

The protest is designed as an “integrity test of the new leadership’s commitment to ending Britain’s complicity in Israel’s ethnic cleansing and war crimes”, they said.

Burnham faced further scrutiny on Friday as Declassified UK, an investigative outlet focused on foreign policy, reported that it had been denied media passes to cover the Labour conference, which runs from Sunday to Wednesday.

Compared with his predecessors, Burnham has taken a stronger stance against illegal Israeli settlements and settler violence in the occupied West Bank, announcing sanctions earlier this month.

But rights groups and activists have called on Labour to suspend all arms sales to Israel in order to stop the bloodshed in Gaza and the West Bank.

They also want the UK to reverse the ban on Palestine Action, whose main target is Israel’s largest weapons maker, Elbit Systems.

“If [prime minister] Burnham means what he says, that he plans to end Britain’s complicity in Israel’s horrific crimes, then he would stop the arrests of people peacefully demonstrating against the genocide and the authoritarian attempts to crush its opponents,” Defend Our Juries said. “We urge PM Burnham to do the only sensible thing and lift the ban on Palestine Action, the very people in the UK actually trying to prevent British complicity in Israel’s war crimes.”

In recent years, the Labour Party has faced waves of criticism over its positions on Israel and Palestine.

“I think the interests of a Labour leader who wants to keep the Labour Party together, and keep a broad electoral bloc together too in a first-past-the-post system, is to try and defang this issue as much as possible,” Colm Murphy, a senior lecturer in British politics at Queen Mary University, told Al Jazeera.

He explained that “we’ve seen a series of gradual steps” on Palestine by party leaders, but the shift has been a “slow, painful evolution”.

“Recognition of the Palestinian state by [former Prime Minister Keir] Starmer was the culmination of a process really begun by Ed Miliband,” he said, referring to the current Foreign Secretary who was Labour’s leader from 2010 until 2015.

Starmer was prime minister when the UK proscribed Palestine Action under the Terrorism Act.

Days after Israel attacked Gaza following the Hamas attacks of October 2023, then-PM Starmer said Israel had the “right” to cut off the strip’s water supply, adding, “Obviously, everything should be done within international law.”

Although he later walked back his statement, for many, the damage was done.

“The legacy of Starmer is actually worsened by the fact that Burnham and Miliband were able to act, because it shows that they could act and they had the political will, they had the personal and public will, and they actually did do something,” said Joseph Willits, head of Parliamentary Affairs at the Council for Arab-British Understanding.

The new sanctions announced under Burnham’s Labour highlight the “inadequacies and the lack of will from the previous government”, he said.

Before Starmer, Jeremy Corbyn, a leftist and lifelong supporter of Palestinian rights, led Labour.

But his era was marred by allegations of anti-Semitism and in late 2019, he announced his resignation as the party’s head.

Under Miliband’s tenure, Labour’s stance on Palestine was supportive of a two-state solution and Palestinian statehood.

He has since reflected on how his Jewish mother, a Holocaust survivor, shaped the principles that have guided him.

The question remains whether Burnham’s Labour could reverse the ban on Palestine Action, especially after United States President Donald Trump recently outlawed the group.

“I think it’s too early to say,” Willits said. “If this is also a battle line with Trump and the Trump administration, do they pick that battle line or the others? Has he already picked other battle lines when it comes to Palestine and therefore does he just leave this one?”

Murphy said Burnham’s Labour may address issues around Palestine Action if they become “salient in British politics again”.

“I’m not so sure it will, but we shall see. A protest might raise the profile a bit.”

articles.title: Europe frets as the Kremlin pushes the limits of its hybrid warfare
articles.summary: The Kremlin is testing Europe‘s limits.
articles.body: The Kremlin is testing Europe‘s limits. After months of covert attacks and sabotage across the continent, leaders are warning that Moscow may be about to grow bolder as it seeks to sow chaos and intimidate allies of Ukraine. Russian President Vladimir Putin could try to test NATO’s resolve to defend members on its eastern flank or respond to attacks that fall short of all-out war, these officials say, at a time when the U.S. is distracted by other conflicts and weighing reducing its military presence in Europe. An assessment by the Danish Defence Intelligence Service released Thursday warned that in the coming months Moscow will further intensify its campaign of so-called hybrid warfare, “with greater consequences for the targeted countries than in the past.” It also assessed “a low but growing risk that Russia will launch a limited military attack against one or several NATO countries bordering Russia.” While Moscow has for years embraced tactics that straddle the threshold of war, a string of increasingly brazen incidents in recent months has alarmed U.S. allies. ‘A bit freaked out’ A key moment was the discovery of a Russian drone carrying explosives at an airport in eastern Germany near a Ukrainian aircraft last month. Berlin formally blamed Russia for what it said was a thwarted attack and imposed a diplomatic freeze, though Moscow denied involvement. That incident appears to have changed the mindset about Russia’s growing threat in Europe, said Ed Arnold, a senior associate fellow in international security at the Royal United Services Institute, a London-based think tank. “It just showed that Putin’s risk calculations are getting more liberal,” Arnold said. “Everyone just got a bit freaked out by that, quite frankly.” It was followed by the unexpected visit of CIA Director John Ratcliffe to Moscow, during which NATO was discussed. Incidents have continued to pile up — at defense facilities in Estonia, rail networks in Poland and the power grid in Germany. Many have passed without clear attribution, only intensifying speculation. All this against the backdrop of near-daily drone incursions into European airspace, fueling anxiety in eastern border towns. In Ukraine, a passenger train was hit less than 2 miles from the Polish border earlier this month, a close call on NATO’s doorstep that came as European diplomats returned from Kyiv on the same rail line. Another train, with former CIA Director David Petraeus on board, was still at the station when the drone struck. Just days later, NATO fighter jets shot down a drone that entered the airspace of Lithuania, one of the Baltic member states whose proximity to Russia, analysts say, could make it a prime target for the Kremlin’s next move. What could this look like? As unease increasingly swirled last week, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the Kremlin plans to launch drone and missile attacks against European countries that it would argue were accidental to try to weaken any response. Russia has not claimed involvement in any of the incidents and has repeatedly denied conducting hybrid warfare or sabotage operations in NATO territory. Putin himself accused European leaders earlier this month of seeking out “a war against Russia” and “frightening their populations with an imaginary threat.” On Friday, Russian state news agency RIA published and quickly deleted an op-ed laying out a potential scenario for a “lightning fast” war that Russia might wage against a NATO state, specifically focusing on the Baltic nations. The article was deleted because it did not “align” with editorial policy or Russia’s state policy, RIA said. U.S. allies have little doubt that the broad pattern reflects the Kremlin increasingly pushing the boundaries. “With these incidents now so frequent and so brazen, it is increasingly difficult to distinguish them from actual acts of war,” said Katja Bego, a senior research fellow with the Europe program at London-based think tank Chatham House. “The Kremlin is playing with fire here: The risk of more serious escalation — even if unintended — is very real.” Baltic states urge caution There is a mounting sense that something must be done, but what? Lithuania has made plans for the evacuation of older adults and is lifting its ban on hosting nuclear weapons. Finland has warned citizens to be “mentally prepared” for new sabotage attacks. France is putting a plan in place to protect the country’s critical infrastructure. Hanging over all of this is Article 5, NATO’s collective defense clause. For Moscow, escalating hybrid attacks could highlight Western divisions over how best to respond and undermine the alliance at a time when the U.S. commitment to this mutual defense has been in question. “I think they are trying to show Europe they can act without consequences, and more recently, to show Europe that the U.S. will not come to their rescue. It’s worrisome,” said William Alberque, a former senior NATO official based in Berlin. Secretary of State Marco Rubio met with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov on Wednesday and told a media briefing that the U.S. was concerned that the Ukraine war could “metastasize and spread into other places ... be it through a hybrid attack, be it through a sabotage attack, be it through a misunderstanding.” He added: “We watch reports carefully, and we raise them with the right people at the right levels.” A State Department spokesperson told NBC News: “We continue to monitor Russia’s hybrid activities in Europe and are working closely with our allies and partners to strengthen resilience against the hybrid threat.” Despite the spreading sense of alarm, some in Europe are urging against getting carried away. NATO’s Baltic member states have not changed their security assessments, saying there is no imminent risk of a Russian invasion while much of Moscow’s military resources are tied up in Ukraine — and struggling to make progress there. Latvia and Estonia directly border Russia, while Lithuania borders the Russian enclave of Kaliningrad. All three have been staunch supporters of Ukraine’s fight, driven in part by fears they could be next. “Incursion of the type of 2022 Ukraine is not likely, let’s put it in a mild way,” Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs told reporters on the sidelines of this week’s United Nations General Assembly in New York. “Ukraine is fighting. Russia is absorbed in Ukraine. We do not observe any build-up near our borders,” Rinkēvičs added. Neighboring Lithuania said this week a new rotation of U.S. troops was on its way to the country, ending uncertainty over a renewed deployment as the Pentagon weighs a broader plan to draw down U.S. forces on the continent. “Russia’s pressure on Lithuania and other countries is not new,” Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas told NBC News, pointing to the decadelong Soviet occupation and adding that his country has more recently faced cyberattacks, disinformation and other forms of hostile influence from Moscow. “There is no conventional threat at the moment,” Kaunas said via email, when asked why his country has not changed its security assessment. “At the same time, provocations and false-flag operations remain possible, and our intelligence points to increasingly aggressive Russian behavior. These are different threats, and they need different answers.” But failing to take sufficient action could carry its own risks. “Respond. Always respond,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy urged his European allies earlier this week. “If you don’t respond to Russians, they will go further.”

articles.title: France’s prestigious Goncourt prize drops novel after author accused of using AI
articles.summary: The organisers of the prestigious Goncourt literary prize said on Friday they had removed a smash-hit novel by Haitian-Canadian author Thelyson Orelien from their longlist after accusations he used AI to write it.
articles.body: The organisers of the prestigious Goncourt literary prize said on Friday they had removed a smash-hit novel by Haitian-Canadian author Thelyson Orelien from their longlist after accusations he used AI to write it. Orelien denied using AI to write “C’etait Ca ou Mourir” (“It Was Either That or Die”) as the allegations ignited a debate about race, literary merit and originality that has roiled the French literary establishment. The accusations about AI use were made this week by a little-known X account “Balance ton Claude.” Essayist Samuel Fitoussi later claimed ownership of the account, saying he managed it with other unidentified individuals. The AI accusations were followed by reports that Orelien had committed plagiarism in earlier works. La Presse said that a 2012 short story by Orelien had plagiarized passages from a book by French author Louis Pauwels, while a 2013 opinion piece copied from The Philippine Star newspaper. Orelien has yet to respond to those accusations, and did not respond to a request for comment on Friday. The Paris-based Academie Goncourt said it had taken note of the AI and plagiarism accusations, and had decided to remove his novel “to preserve the integrity of the Goncourt Prize and that of the Academie, whose central role is to promote and honour literature written by women and men.” The Academie said it hoped its decision would show it was fully against the “creation of texts generated with the assistance of AI,” adding it would make no further comment before October 6, when it will announce its shortlist. The debut novel by the Haitian-born author tells the story of a Haitian migrant who travels north through Latin America before ending up in Canada. It has won a host of other literary awards, and was due to be translated into multiple languages. His French and Canadian publishers initially offered Orelien their full support over the AI allegations. They did not respond to requests for comment on Friday. “Balance ton Claude” said that running passages through AI detection tool Pangram showed the novel “was written almost entirely by artificial intelligence”. Some experts say the reliability of AI detection tools is questionable.

articles.title: Thai capital Bangkok declared disaster zone amid widespread flooding
articles.summary: Bangkok’s governor on Saturday declared Thailand’s capital city a disaster-affected zone after torrential rain led to widespread flooding, while the weather agency forecast thunderstorms ​over the weekend.
articles.body: Bangkok’s governor on Saturday declared Thailand’s capital city a disaster-affected zone after torrential rain led to widespread flooding, while the weather agency forecast thunderstorms ​over the weekend. Major roads were flooded with cars partly submerged and ​people were forced to wade through waist-height water after nearly ⁠300mm (12 inches) of rain fell within 48 hours. Bangkok Governor Chadchart ​Sittipunt said the crisis “poses a risk to people’s lives” and could damage ​public and private property, and that the situation was most severe near canals. The army said it is setting up shelters and field kitchens among other disaster relief efforts, ​while the Bangkok Metropolitan Administration has designated schools as temporary accommodation ​and asked residents to avoid unnecessary travel. Supermarkets were crowded with people stocking up on ‌supplies. “I’m ⁠worried too, because I haven’t stocked up on food beforehand, and I’ve never faced this kind of situation alone before, since my parents aren’t with me,” said 19-year-old Sansuk Laowatcharakul. The government on Saturday issued an emergency ​advisory for people living ​near canals ⁠to move possessions to higher ground. Before the warning, “I wasn’t aware enough to consider relocating,” said Bangkok resident Suppakarn ​Julavijitphong as he carried luggage from a condo surrounded ​by floodwater. The ⁠city’s main airport, Suvarnabhumi, was operating normally though the tourism authority advised travellers to allow an extra two to three hours in their plans. Thailand experienced ⁠its worst ​floods in decades in November when at ​least 145 people died and thousands of homes were damaged in the southern provinces.

articles.title: Trump ‘rejects’ Iran’s seven-day ceasefire proposal. What’s next?
articles.summary: Analysts say Trump may opt to resume attacks on Iran after November midterm elections.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump has reportedly ruled out an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within a week, according to unnamed US officials cited by The Wall Street Journal.

Trump’s rejection comes just hours after Iran put forward a new roadmap to opening the strait, through which one-fifth of global oil and natural gas is shipped during peacetime – and days after the US president threatened to “annihilate” Iran from the floor of the UN General Assembly.

Here’s what we know about Trump’s response to the proposal and what could come next in the conflict.

The proposal lays out a roadmap to open the Strait of Hormuz with normal maritime passage within a week.

Speaking to reporters on Friday, Iran’s Foreign Minister, Abbas Araghchi, said the proposal calls for the US to take actions it committed to under the failed June 17 Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) on an accelerated timeframe.

Those actions include releasing $12bn in frozen Iranian assets, lifting Iranian oil sanctions and ending the US’s naval blockade on Iranian ports, Araghchi told reporters at a private media briefing on Thursday, according to The New York Times. He also said all hostilities, including in Lebanon, where Israel still occupies part of the south of the country, must cease during the seven-day period.

Araghchi said once the US conditions are met – which he estimated would take four or five days – the Strait of Hormuz could be reopened and negotiations with the US on a “final deal” would start on day seven.

He said the process could begin as soon as the US accepts the plan.

“The choice now rests with the United States,” said Araghchi. “Iran does not accept coercion, threats or intimidation.”

The US government has not publicly responded to the plan.

However, The Wall Street Journal reported that Trump had quickly ruled it out, citing unnamed US officials.

They said Trump was sceptical about whether Iran would fulfil US demands. Trump’s most persistent demands have been that Iran never be able to acquire a nuclear weapon and that it restore free passage in Hormuz.

Iran says it will not discuss its nuclear programme until the conditions it has laid down are met, which has led to an impasse between the two sides.

Meanwhile, a US official has told Al Jazeera that Washington is in no hurry to respond to Iran’s proposal and that it sees itself as being in a strong position with respect to the Strait of Hormuz.

Late on Friday night, Trump posted an image of a map on his Truth Social platform that labelled it “Trump Strait”.

Trump has previously said the US has “total control” over the waterway and threatened to designate it as a US territory . Iran strongly denied that, saying it has complete control of the strait.

Yes, but mostly indirectly. At the UN General Assembly in New York this week, Qatar has been passing messages between the two sides as an intermediary.

Both the US and Iran have said the door to diplomacy remains open and a US official told Al Jazeera that ongoing mediated talks are “positive and constructive”.

Qatar, a key mediator in the conflict, said its foreign minister spoke with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Friday about de-escalation and the conditions for renewed dialogue.

Earlier this week, US officials, including special envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, held mediated discussions with Iranian counterparts in New York, a meeting Trump described as “very good”.

Nevertheless, there is “an enormous amount of scepticism in Washington that the two countries are on the same page,” according to Thomas Warrick, senior fellow at the Atlantic Council.

“I think that the best we can hope for is that this offer from the Iranian foreign minister does lead to further discussions to try to clarify what preconditions Washington is willing to work with,” Warrick told Al Jazeera.

Where does the US-Iran standoff go from here?

According to the US officials cited in The Wall Street Journal, Trump told his aides he expects to carry out a new bombing campaign against Iran after the US midterm elections in November.

That comes after Trump told the UN General Assembly he was considering whether to “annihilate” Iran and “drive them into hell” in the absence of a deal.

At the same time, Trump has said he believes a deal to end the conflict will come shortly after the midterms.

Paul Musgrave, an associate professor of government at Georgetown University in Qatar, told Al Jazeera that Trump “doesn’t want to end the war on unfavourable terms” and that the result of November’s elections will likely help steer his policy.

If Trump’s Republican party suffers severe setbacks in the elections – and loses its majority in Congress – he may opt for “unilateral actions, including perhaps a resumption of warfare”, said Musgrave.

“That would also mean that Iran would have delivered a really stinging political blow to President Trump,” Musgrave continued, adding this could trigger short-term escalation, “followed by negotiation so that the White House doesn’t look like it’s just surrendering”.

articles.title: Iran says choice on reopening Hormuz ‘rests with the United States’ after deal offer
articles.summary: The choice to reopen the Strait of Hormuz “rests with the United States,” Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Friday, indicating shipping through the critical waterway could resume within days once a deal is reached.
articles.body: The choice to reopen the Strait of Hormuz “rests with the United States,” Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Friday, indicating shipping through the critical waterway could resume within days once a deal is reached. “If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened, and normal maritime passage restored within seven days,” Araghchi told reporters. “The choice now rests with the United States.” He said a “concrete seven-day plan” had been conveyed to the U.S. through Qatar, after indirect talks through mediators were held on the sidelines of this week’s United Nations General Assembly in New York. “The seven day timeline starts as soon as the United States accepts this plan,” he added. “If they accept this plan tomorrow, the seven days will start from tomorrow. There are certain actions to be taken by the United States. And we believe that these actions can be taken in four or five days.” Araghchi said that the actions required by the U.S. in their proposal were already agreed to in the June Memorandum of Understanding between the two countries that laid out plans for a temporary ceasefire. That agreement, signed in June, collapsed within days after fresh strikes were exchanged. “They fall already under the commitments of the United States, so we don’t see any difficulty to implement them,” he said. One of the conditions of the plan is for the U.S. to accept a maritime transit route through the Strait of Hormuz that has been agreed upon by Iran and Oman, Araghchi said Thursday. A U.S. official said the Trump Administration is having positive and constructive discussions through the mediators but that they were not in any hurry to reach an agreement. “The United States is in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz, so we are not in a rush,” the U.S. official said. “Over the last 48 hours, nearly 40 million barrels of oil have transited the Strait.” Early Saturday, President Donald Trump posted an image to Truth Social of the Strait of Hormuz labelled the “Trump Strait.” Earlier this week, he had said he was still considering whether to “annihilate” Iran or make a deal. In an interview with Al Jazeera on Saturday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said that resolving the Hormuz issue “is possible through negotiations, not the use of force,” but warned that his country does not “trust” talks with Washington. Trump has repeatedly said that the goal of attacking Iran was to prevent the development of a nuclear weapon. Soon after the war started, Iran blocked the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway through which some 20% of the world’s oil flowed before the conflict, sending shock waves through the world economy. Polls show Democrats with an advantage heading into the November contests. The latest NBC News Decision Desk Poll found 31% of respondents approved of Trump’s handling of the Iran war, while 69% disapproved. Pezeshkian on Thursday suggested his government was willing to make a deal with the U.S. to end the war before Americans head to the polls this November. “We don’t want it to get to the midterm elections,” Pezeshkian said in a brief meeting with NBC News and other news organizations, two days after Trump said that he believed the Iranian regime would not make a deal to settle the conflict until after November’s elections. “I believe we’ll make a deal right after the election because it doesn’t make sense for them not to,” Trump said. “They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election.” The U.S. this week announced it would put sanctions on any global companies doing business ​with Iranian airlines, with the aim of grounding Iran’s entire civil fleet worldwide. Iraq said Saturday that it was engaging with the U.S. in an effort to restore humanitarian flights to and from Iran, after Iranian airlines were barred from neighboring countries in response to the sanctions. Efforts were ongoing to “secure exemptions for certain Iraqi airports from these measures” in order to enable “the resumption of flights for humanitarian reasons, such as medical treatment, education, religious pilgrimages, and the interests of civilians,” the Iraqi prime minister’s office said. Iran’s Tasnim news agency reported that flights had also been shut down to Oman, Georgia and Azerbaijan.

articles.summary: Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif's address at the United Nations General Assembly, in which he sought to reiterate Islamabad's false narrative on
articles.body: Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif's address at the United Nations General Assembly, in which he sought to reiterate Islamabad's false narrative on the 2025 conflict with India, drew a viral reaction from an Indian diplomat.The cameras captured Indian diplomat R Srinivas appearing to smirk and laugh as Sharif spoke about Pakistan’s claimed “victory” in the May 2025 conflict with India.The moment came as Sharif presented Islamabad’s version of the conflict and raised several issues concerning India, including the Indus Waters Treaty and Kashmir.Addressing the UN, Sharif praised US President Donald Trump for his role in preventing further escalation between the two nuclear-armed neighbours during Operation Sindoor.“His timely intervention came at a decisive juncture when two nuclear-armed neighbours stood at the brink of an all-out war. And, who knows, Mr President, the extent of devastation that could have taken place had President Trump not stepped in at this critical moment with clarity of thought and action,” Sharif said.“Mr President, we must therefore ensure that South Asia never reaches that precipice ever again,” he added.India, however, has consistently maintained that the cessation of military action on May 10, 2025, was reached through direct communication between India and Pakistan and did not involve third-party mediation.Pakistan’s Director General of Military Operations (DGMO) had approached his Indian counterpart on May 10, seeking a cessation of military action.India had launched Operation Sindoor on May 7, 2025, following the April 22 Pahalgam terror attack that killed 26 people. India said the operation targeted terrorist infrastructure in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir.India also exercised its right of reply to Sharif’s remarks. Petal Gahlot, First Secretary in India’s Permanent Mission to the UN, criticised Pakistan’s political system and its references to democratic rights and human values. She also referred to Osama bin Laden’s presence near Pakistan’s military academy.“This afternoon, the General Assembly heard some bizarre remarks from the representative of Pakistan. This happens just a fortnight after New York City and the world marked the 25th anniversary of the horrendous 9-11 terrorist attack. This context is important to keep in mind because its mastermind, Osama bin Laden, was living right on the doorstep of the Pakistani Army's premier academy. This was the very entity which was the subject of such deep genuflection before us today by the representative of Pakistan. But all this is only to be expected from what Pakistanis themselves call a Form 47 government.”Gahlot also responded to Pakistan’s references to democratic rights and the role of the military in the country. “We heard some hypocritical homilies about democratic rights and human values from a regime whose capital at this very moment is being fortified against its own people. And that, Mr. President, is happening because this is a regime of the army, by the army, and for the army. Their puppets may come and go, but let us have no illusion about who calls the shots. The reality of Pakistan is expressed in its 27th Amendment and the lifelong immunity granted to its real ruler," she added.Sharif also criticised India’s decision to place the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance, arguing that the “move was not legal” and highlighting the importance of the Indus river system to Pakistan.India placed the treaty in abeyance following the Pahalgam terror attack and has said the decision will remain in effect until Pakistan takes credible and irreversible action against cross-border terrorism.
