articles.title: ‘Marie Antoinette’ at 20: A peak behind the velvet curtain
articles.summary: At the Cannes Film Festival in 2006 the movie was booed by viewers and panned by critics. Now, it’s a cult classic.
articles.body: Sofia Coppola was once robbed. The burglar broke into the first floor of the director’s New York townhouse, scanned an array of expensive framed artworks on her wall and made their choice. It was a little surprising. The thief decided to steal a set photo of Coppola’s 2006 movie, “Marie Antoinette.” In it, two extras stand in a large white tent, dressed in designer Milena Canonero’s pastel Oscar-winning costumes, snapping a photo on a digital camera. “It’s so funny because you can watch the surveillance camera and the guy looks around and around and that’s the thing he takes,” said the creator of the image, Andrew Durham, a photographer, producer and close friend of Coppola’s, in a video call. “Like why? I don’t know. It’s such a random thing.” Maybe the robber was a film student. Or at least had an active Tumblr account in the 2010s — where Durham’s intimate behind-the-scenes photographs of Coppola’s third feature film had fostered a cult audience. Fascination around Coppola’s stylish, sympathetic biopic of the Dauphine of France has hardly waned in the 20 years since its release. So much so, it’s hard to envision the film’s once rocky start. At the Cannes Film Festival in 2006 the movie was booed by viewers and panned by critics. The Guardian called it “baffling and historically obtuse,” while Slate said Coppola was “as nostalgic about the ancien régime as ‘Gone with the Wind’ is about the antebellum South.” Much of the outrage pivoted on the film’s disinterest in accuracy, from the new wave romantic soundtrack to the American accents. It didn’t help that Coppola had been granted unique access to actually film inside the Palace of Versailles, a privilege some believed was totally wasted. The movie covered its production costs at box office, but not much more. It didn’t go entirely without industry recognition, however. Canonero won the Oscar for best costume design for her froo-froo pastel creations in 2007, and the movie even took home the Cinema Prize of the French National Education System at Cannes — a surprising bolt of irony, considering many initial complaints were leveled at the film’s departure from historical events. Some critics did get on board with Coppola’s vision, and praised her accordingly. But over time, the tide has turned completely. Now, “Marie Antoinette” is lauded as the film that launched a new chapter of vibes-based period dramas, legitimizing directors more interested in conjuring a mood than chronicled truth. Powdered wigs and iPod classics The film has taken on a more mythologized afterlife beyond its initial release, becoming a cultural shorthand for gilded loneliness and the young queen a melancholic symbol of girlhood. Last year, London’s V&A museum staged a multi-roomed menagerie of the young queen’s clothes, shoes and bedroom furniture, as well as Canonero’s costumes and a collection of contemporary runway pieces that took inspiration from the Dauphine herself. Curator Sarah Grant said the showcase “wouldn’t have been possible” without Coppola’s movie. This week, Versailles opened its own exhibition, more tightly focused on the film; while next month, “Marie Antoinette” is set to receive a full theatrical re-release to celebrate 20 years. If that wasn’t enough, fans can now re-live life on Coppola’s set through not one, but two pieces of media that immortalized every pannier and pastry. The first is Durham’s enormous collection of point-and-shoot film photos, and the second is the late Eleanor Coppola’s behind-the-scenes documentary, “Making Marie Antoinette,” released next month. Durham took 1,872 photos, to be exact, across 52 rolls. The final book, published this month by Important Flowers, is a curated selection of around 400 images. “I was really there just to document the production for Sofia,” Durham said. “Just for our archives, so Sofia and I could have all these snapshots.” He flew out from Los Angeles to Paris, crashed on Coppola’s sofa and traveled with her each morning to set. “Luckily for me, no one was doing what I was doing, and nobody cared,” he said. “I just walked around with my camera and sort of did my thing,” he added. His ‘thing’ was often zoning in on the pleasingly incongruous, particularly moments where 18th century dress clashed with early 2000’s tech — Kirsten Dunst and Jason Schwartzman in full costume using an Apple PowerBook, or sharing headphones plugged into an iPod Classic, or extras in powdered wigs smoking and talking on a brick phone. Durham’s pictures were first published by Vogue France, and then other magazines around the world became interested — they were licensed at first legally, with the help of a syndicate agent he had proactively sought-out. Then, after the invention of social media, the photos popped up anywhere and everywhere. “We had no control over them,” he said. The images have been printed onto bootleg T-shirts and circulate endlessly on the internet. “I’d see this photo of Jason and Kirsten on this Vespa, it was everywhere,” he said. “And I was like, I don’t know how people got it.” A different era Part of the reason Durham believes these photos have had such a long tail is the fact they act as a kind of “time capsule.” “This movie was shot the year before the iPhone came out,” he said. “I think that says a lot about what these images represent.” There’s also an undercurrent of indie sleaze zeitgeist. “Maybe for young people they represent this cool older movie,” Durham added. “It’s kind of fun seeing these actors when they were younger and everyone’s smoking and it evokes a different era.” There is something debauched and luxurious about Durham’s photos, and not just because everyone in them is dressed as French aristocrats guzzling champagne and popping bon-bons. Today, the US film industry has battled a downward spiral with around 30% unemployment since 2022 according to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Studios are making significantly fewer movies than even just a few years ago, and declining film budgets mean it’s hard to get a film financed at all — let alone money for extra niceties. “When I arrived in Paris, I felt like the film set just mirrored the court of Versailles,” said Durham. “We would have these fabulous long lunches… Then it spilled out into our weekends and days off.” Photos of the cast and crew dancing at Le Baron, their “go-to hangout,” are peppered throughout the book — including a bleary-eyed photo of Coppola in the wee hours of the morning locked outside the apartment because Durham lost the keys on the dance floor. “We were all just a bunch of kids having fun in Paris,” he said. A mother’s perspective Durham’s approach to documenting was different to that of Eleanor Coppola, the late documentary filmmaker who died in 2024 and Sofia Coppola’s mother, who filmed her own version of events on set. Sofia and Eleanor Coppola began working on the commemorative documentary together while quarantining together during 2020’s COVID-19 pandemic, with Sofia ultimately finishing the film following her mother’s death. “She was one of the most stealth people,” said Durham. “My process was more just going out and befriending people.” His pocket-sized Contax TVS3 meant he could snap photos quickly in a way that wasn’t intrusive, he said. “Eleanor, she was tucked away and so quiet, you don’t even know she’s there. Her process was so different, it was like a fly on the wall.” Eleanor Coppola captured over 80 hours of footage from the movie’s time in production — recording intimate moments on set including her daughter’s brief flares of frustration with man-splaining colleagues, or Dunst’s polite ambivalence at being filmed for an additional project in-between takes. But more than just letting fans re-experience “Marie Antoinette” through a candid lens, the documentary allows viewers to see the whole thing from a mother’s singular point-of-view. Actor Diane Lane narrates passages of Coppola’s own diary throughout the film where she recalls the immensity of witnessing her daughter’s professional and creative ambition first-hand. The final shot of the documentary shows Dunst luxuriating in a bathtub reciting one of history’s most fictionalized quips — “let them eat cake.” It was, fittingly, the last scene filmed on set in Versailles. Eleanor Coppola’s narration tells us that Sofia was astonished that they not only managed to finish the film, but also do so on time and on budget. Small-scale wins that pale in comparison to the film’s place in cinematic history. “I don’t know if people can afford to make movies like that,” said Durham of Sofia Coppola’s masterpiece. “This really feels like the kind of movie that has gone out of style.”

articles.title: Mount Shasta climber recounts harrowing 500-foot slide, overnight crawl to safety: report
articles.summary: Zubayir Kazi lost all his supplies during a failed glissade down Mount Shasta's Avalanche Gulch and crawled through the night with grave injuries.
articles.body: A California climber who survived a roughly 500-foot slide down Mount Shasta is recounting how he crawled through the night after losing his supplies and suffering serious injuries. Zubayir Kazi, 24, of San Jose, told NBC Bay Area that he reached the summit Sept. 10, during his first icy summit attempt before things went wrong on his descent. "Everything I had with me just goes out of my hand and I find myself flying down the mountain," Kazi said. NOVICE CLIMBER SURVIVES 1,500-FOOT DROP ON CALIFORNIA'S MOUNT SHASTA AFTER HELICOPTER RESCUE DELAYED BY CLOUDS Kazi said he lost his food, water, cellphone and light, leaving him alone without a way to call for help. "My mentality became very one dimensional. I don’t know what’s the optimal thing to do, but I just know that I have to go lower because if I stay here and fall asleep, I’m going to die," he said. The U.S. Forest Service previously told Fox News Digital that Kazi lost control while attempting to glissade, or slide, down the snow and ice-covered Avalanche Gulch after reaching the summit. He suffered significant lacerations and injuries to his feet. NURSE IMPALED BY POLE DURING HIKE FORCED TO TREK 10 MILES FOR HELP: 'A FREAK THING' Swelling forced Kazi to remove his boots, and he crawled through the night until reaching Horse Camp Cabin. His friends reported him missing after losing contact with him, prompting a multi-agency search. A hiker found Kazi inside the cabin the following day and provided him with food and water before rescuers arrived. "When the officers came in, it was the first time I really realized how badly I was injured. They said 'You have no skin behind your leg'," Kazi said. HIKER, 61, BATTLES AGONIZING INJURY ON GRUELING CLIMB, RESETS DISLOCATED SHOULDER HIMSELF Kazi told NBC Bay Area that he suffered significant skin and nerve damage and serious internal complications. He said doctors told him he could have died within hours. The Forest Service previously praised Kazi for knowing his route and telling friends about his climbing plans, while urging climbers to carry backup electronics, allow enough daylight and prepare to self-rescue. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Kazi said the ordeal changed his approach to climbing. "It is very important to fully and properly account for all of the requirements and safety considerations necessary to complete a hike like this and not miss a single one — and I'd say to definitely not go alone," Kazi said. Fox News Digital could not locate contact information for Kazi to seek additional comment. Fox News Digital's Bonny Chu contributed to this report.

articles.title: Meet Sophie Kim, the California teen who turned an online climate-anxiety group into a youth nonprofit with 700+ members in 30+ countries and won a $10,000 national young hero prize
articles.summary: For many young people, the climate crisis did not come as a distant scientific issue but as something deeply personal.
articles.body: For many young people, the climate crisis did not come as a distant scientific issue but as something deeply personal. Wildfires, extreme weather and an uncertain future could make an already complex world feel even more overwhelming. For Sophie Kim, that anxiety became the impetus to build a community, rather than retreat from the problem. The 18-year-old California student has turned an online community started during the Covid pandemic into The Clean & Green Initiative (TCAGI), a youth-led environmental nonprofit with more than 700 members in more than 30 countries. The work has now garnered national recognition, including a spot on the 2026 recipients of the Barron Prize for Young Heroes and a $10,000 national young hero prize, the National Society of High School Scholars website report states.From environmental anxiety to environmental actionTCAGI began with a straightforward, but audacious, idea: how to help children understand climate change without scaring them with it. Sophie’s own experience of eco-anxiety as a child inspired the organization’s first major project, a series of children’s books aimed at introducing the climate crisis to young readers while emphasizing hope, teamwork and practical action. The first book, Stella and the Starlight Solution, is about Stella the Star visiting Earth and learning her friend is in trouble. A friendly alien helps her understand what is happening and introduces her to the mysterious Starlight Solution. Along the way, Stella meets people who are helping the planet in different ways, and slowly learns that the solution is not one magic answer, but collective action. The book combines environmental facts with vibrant visuals and an approachable story, giving children an entry point into what can otherwise be an overwhelming topic.A global network of young peopleThe project quickly grew beyond the initial book project. Sophie gathered 32 young people from 14 countries to help develop TCAGI’s projects and promote environmental awareness. Their work ranges from writing and illustrating Stella and the Starlight Solution to producing blogs, creating social media content, contributing to YouTube and managing the organization’s Discord community.Since then TCAGI has attracted more than 700 members from over 30 countries. Its work has been funded and supported by organizations such as DoSomething.org, the Jane Goodall Institute and Bow Seat Ocean Awareness. The initiative has also been covered in publications by Blue Shield and Project Green Schools.From creativity to conservationAnother of Sophie’s major projects has been the Sounds, Scenes, & Stories of Nature Contest, co-developed with Bow Seat and its mentors. The international contest asked participants to submit creative work that celebrated nature, from photography and poetry to other art forms. After a slow start, the contest eventually attracted more than 600 entries from 14 countries. Sophie is currently working on a book to display the winning entries, which will take the message of the project beyond the competition itself. She is also developing a jewelry line, with the intention of donating 100% of the proceeds to Ukrainian charities, including UNITED24 and Maya’s Hope.Several causesSophie is more than an environmental activist. She started the Bipartisan Bridges program, which brings together high school students for structured debates on social topics. Her ever-expanding work has earned her a spot as one of the 2026 Barron Prize Young Heroes, an award recognizing young people for their initiative and impact in their communities. For Sophie, the journey that began with eco-anxiety has transformed into something much larger, a network where young people can learn, create and take action together. As she prepares to continue her environmental work in college, TCAGI’s story gives us a glimpse into what can happen when fear becomes the spark for building something constructive.Images Courtesy: istock and NSHSSYou use AI every day. articles.title: An unexpected welcome: Syrian Kurds return to their homes in Afrin
articles.summary: Syrian Kurds are beginning to return to their homes in Afrin after years in exile, but have different experiences.
articles.body:
Afrin, Syria – When Dilshad Hamdo walked into the home his father built 30 years ago, there was no place to sit. The stone walls were intact, but the rooms had been stripped bare. Yet, standing in the empty space, there was still a strong sense of relief at being back home.

“I have a lot of memories in this house with my extended family. There is nothing like the house and the land,” Hamdo told Al Jazeera.

Hamdo fled Afrin as a young man in early 2018, during a Turkish-led military offensive, dubbed “Operation Olive Branch”, against the Kurdish-dominated People’s Protection Units (YPG) of the Syrian Democratic Forces.

In the ensuing chaos, tens of thousands of Syrian Kurds were displaced. Vacant properties across Afrin were soon occupied by other displaced Syrians, most of them Arabs fleeing the intense Syrian government bombardments of opposition areas in Homs and Damascus.

For the Hamdos, exile meant drifting ever eastwards – from Aleppo to Raqqa of Syria, and finally to a camp for the displaced in Qamishli.

“We heard that there are people returning to Afrin, and that there is registration in order to return,” Hamdo recalled. “We told them we want to return to our land. We cannot live here. Because a person can only rest in his house and his land, and we suffered greatly outside our land.”

Following the collapse of Bashar al-Assad’s regime in December 2024, Syria’s newly formed transitional government announced it would facilitate the safe return of those who had fled Afrin in 2018.

Internal security forces assisted the return of hundreds of Syrian Kurdish families from Hasakah to Afrin in April and May.

Hamdo’s father travelled ahead to check on their property, only to find a displaced family from Homs living inside. Rather than a confrontation, the encounter between the two displaced families ended in a quiet negotiation.

“The people who were living in our house asked for a period of several months until they left. After several months, we paid them 300 American dollars so they would leave the house, travel money so they could return to Homs, and we got our house,” he said.

“After Syria was liberated, we wanted to return to our land. We do not see any distinction between the Arab and the Kurd, and all of us are one people. And we only want peace and safety.”

The transitional government in Damascus is heavily promoting the return of families such as the Hamdos.

Khayro Dawood, the director of the Afrin region, said the state’s priority is to “completely stop the Syrian bleeding” by reaching out to those languishing in camps.

“The state was trying to understand and to receive with an open heart,” Dawood told Al Jazeera, describing government delegations sent to camps in the northeast. “Our visit to the Hasakah region gave a positive impression in the hearts of the people there … and this visit had a positive result in rebuilding trust anew.”

What started as a trial run of 400 families has grown into a wave of roughly 12,000 families returning to Afrin via state-organised convoys.

Dawood pointed to the implementation of Decree 13 – a transitional law recognising the cultural and political rights of Syria’s Kurdish community – as proof of a new era between Arabs and Kurds in Syria.

But government decrees offer little comfort to those returning to homes that lie in ruins.

Zeina Sido boarded one of the recent state-sponsored convoys back to Afrin. “It was a wonderful feeling when they told us, ‘Pack your belongings; you will return to your homes,'” she recalled. “Their treatment was excellent.”

That joy vanished the moment she arrived at her property. Her four-room house had been gutted, looted, and repurposed.

“We went and saw our house completely destroyed,” Sido said. “We found it had turned into a house for sheep. This house was for a human being and it should not turn into a house for animals. Did they not take into consideration that the people of these houses would return to them?”

With no money to rebuild, Sido now lives in a nearby displacement camp – a facility recently vacated by those fleeing the former regime, which is now filling up again with Afrin’s native residents.

“Every time we are able to establish something, we are forced into displacement and we repeat the cycle,” she said

While Sido has bitter feelings about returning home to find nothing as it was, being surrounded by the wreckage of her old life, she refuses to leave the region again.

“My wish is that we establish our family in our house and in our land, and this is a beautiful feeling that we are able to do that,” Sido said. “I still have hope to do that. Were it not for hope, we would not have been able to return here in the first place.”

articles.title: Don’t throw away banana peels: 5 easy ways to turn them into natural plant fertiliser at home
articles.summary: Banana peels often end up in the bin after the fruit is eaten, but they can be reused in the garden instead.
articles.body: Banana peels often end up in the bin after the fruit is eaten, but they can be reused in the garden instead. With a few simple steps, the peels can be turned into banana water, dried pieces, or a fine powder for plants. These homemade preparations are easy to make and require ingredients that are commonly available at home. Banana peels contain nutrients such as potassium, phosphorus, calcium, and magnesium, making them useful as an occasional plant supplement. Gardeners can soak chopped peels in water, dry them before adding them to soil, or grind them into a powder. However, banana peel preparations are not a complete fertiliser and should be used alongside regular plant care.5 ways to make banana peel fertiliser at homeSoak banana peels in water for an easy plant feedCut banana peels into small pieces and place them in a clean jar or container. Add enough water to completely cover the pieces and leave the mixture for two to three days. Strain out the peels before using the liquid on plants. The leftover pieces do not need to be thrown away and can be added to compost. This method is one of the simplest ways to reuse banana peels because it requires no special equipment or complicated preparation.Boil banana peels for a liquid feedBanana peels can also be used to prepare a liquid feed by combining soaking and boiling. Cut the peels into small pieces and soak them in water for two to three days. The softened pieces can then be boiled for around 30 to 45 minutes. Once the liquid has cooled completely, strain it before use. The resulting liquid should be diluted with fresh water rather than being applied directly in a concentrated form.Dry banana peels before using themInstead of making a liquid, gardeners can dry banana peels and use them directly in the soil. Cut the peels into small pieces and place them in sunlight or dry them in an oven at a low temperature. They need to become completely dry before storage or use. Once dry, the pieces can be added around plants or incorporated into the growing medium. This method takes longer to prepare but creates a form that can be stored and used later.Turn dried peels into powderCompletely dried banana peels can be ground into a powder using a blender, food processor, or coffee grinder. The peels should be dry and brittle before grinding so they break down easily. The resulting powder can be mixed into soil or combined with water before being applied to plants. Powdering the peels makes them easier to handle and distribute in smaller quantities. It also provides another way to reuse banana waste without keeping fresh peels around the plants.Try fermented banana peel liquidA fermented preparation takes longer but can also be made at home. One method uses ripe banana pieces and dark brown sugar in equal amounts. The mixture is placed in a container and left for about two weeks to ferment. The resulting liquid is a concentrate and needs to be diluted before it is given to plants. Because fermented mixtures contain sugars, they can attract flies or other insects. This method therefore requires more care than simple banana peel water.5 things to know before using banana peel fertiliserDilute banana peel water before using itBanana peel water should be diluted before it is applied to plants. A simple approach is to mix one part prepared banana water with five parts fresh water. This creates a weaker solution that can be used around the soil instead of applying a concentrated mixture. Dilution is particularly useful when gardeners are trying the preparation for the first time. The diluted liquid can then be added during normal watering rather than being poured directly onto leaves or stems.Use banana water once a weekBanana water does not need to be used every time a plant is watered. Once a week is generally enough for this type of homemade plant feed. Plants still need ordinary water according to their individual requirements, especially during hot or dry weather. Increasing the amount of banana water simply because a plant needs more moisture is not advisable. It is better to keep the banana preparation as an occasional supplement while regular watering continues according to the plant's needs.Use it for suitable houseplants and garden plantsBanana water can be used with a range of plants, including several common houseplants and garden varieties. Pothos, snake plants, monsteras, philodendrons, anthuriums, orchids, tomatoes, bell peppers, roses, ferns, and okra are among the plants that can receive diluted banana water. However, every plant has different watering and nutrient requirements. Gardeners should consider the needs of each plant instead of assuming that the same amount of banana water will work equally well for every pot.Be careful with succulentsSucculents generally require less water and fertiliser than many leafy houseplants. If banana water is used for succulents, it should be diluted and applied carefully. The growing medium should not remain excessively wet. This is especially important because succulents are adapted to conditions where water is less available.Do not use it as a complete fertiliserBanana peel preparations provide only a limited range and amount of nutrients, so they should not replace a complete plant fertiliser. Flowering plants, vegetables and fruiting plants can have higher or more specific nutritional requirements that homemade banana water cannot meet on its own. Using banana peel preparations as an occasional supplement is a more suitable approach. Plants still need appropriate soil, light, water, and a balanced supply of essential nutrients for healthy growth.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: How one of the most bombed places on the planet survived
articles.summary: In our roundup of travel stories this week: Istanbul’s Ottoman legacy, ancient human footprints in New Mexico, and an incredible story of survival during the Vietnam War.
articles.body: We have a history theme to our CNN Travel newsletter this week, from Istanbul’s Ottoman legacy, to the discovery of ancient human footprints in New Mexico, to an underground Nazi fortress in Poland. First up, though, is an incredible story of survival during the Vietnam War. Wartime tunnels and bunkers Before 1965, Vịnh Mốc was a tranquil fishing village in central Vietnam, with a lush landscape of rice paddies, bamboo thickets and golden beaches. Then, due to its strategic location on the border of North and South Vietnam, it became one of the most bombed places on the planet during the Vietnam War. Over eight years, American forces would drop an estimated 9,000 tons of explosives over the village. Relocation wasn’t an option under such heavy bombardment, so villagers took refuge in the only place they could: underground. Within two years, an ingenious tunnel complex was constructed, with arched ceilings and thick walls, and zigzag subterranean pathways to better absorb bomb blasts. Hundreds of residents would spend six years beneath the village while it was under fire, and at least 17 children were born in the underground complex’s maternity ward. Read the full story here. For CNN subscribers, we also have the story of Poland’s Wolin Island, an idyllic vacation getaway, which once housed an underground Nazi fortress. It was an ambitious design, with a network of bunkers and almost a mile of tunnels. The complex, known today as Wolin Underground City, was built secretly by the Nazis in 1936 in defiance of the Versailles Treaty, which prohibited German rearmament after World War I. Today, it’s open for all to see. Ancient footprints and Bronze Age art Experts didn’t believe marks uncovered by a biologist in New Mexico’s White Sands National Park in 2009 were ancient human footprints. Seven years later though, they were proved wrong — and it had earth-shattering consequences for long-debated theories about when prehistoric people first arrived in the Americas. That was just the beginning: The discoveries snowballed from there. Kyrgyzstan’s Saimaluu Tash valley is also home to ancient wonders that only came to light in modern times. Ten thousand rocks, etched with nearly 90,000 carvings dating as far back as the Bronze Age, make Saimaluu Tash one of the largest and most remote high-altitude petroglyph sites in the world. Getting there involves climbing a rocky path through the Tian-Shan mountains and crossing a seasonal snow bridge where the petroglyphs can be accessed for just a fleeting six-week window each summer. For subscribers, the CNN Original Series “The Wonder List with Bill Weir” debuted in 2015 with a visit to the Pacific island of Vanuatu, where native tribes were facing a modern world that threatened their culture’s ancient traditions. Stream the episode here. Istanbul, city of empires The city now known as Istanbul has been at the heart of empires, from the Roman to the Byzantine to the Ottoman, and their legacies can be found throughout the Turkish metropolis. Yedikule Fortress, a former prison and imperial treasury whose origins go back to the fourth-century Walls of Constantinople, is returning to its former magnificence as the result of a multi-stage restoration project. Topkapi Palace, built in the 15th century on a strategic promontory at the edge of Europe, was the seat of the Ottoman Empire for nearly 400 years. It’s one of the world’s greatest surviving palaces, alongside other regal estates such as France’s Palace of Versailles and China’s Forbidden City, and many tales of intrigue between sultans, eunuchs, concubines and the royal household went on within its walls. Wild West movie ranch LA’s Melody Ranch has spent more than a century standing in for America’s Wild West. Its dusty main street, saloon and hand-painted signs are seen in “Gunsmoke,” “Deadwood,” “Django Unchained,” “Westworld” and “Once Upon a Time … in Hollywood.” In case you missed it Thousands of Americans are giving up their citizenship. Here’s why. The world’s best airline for 2026 has been named. It’s a sixth-time win for the elite carrier. A media battle. A food recall. A travel nightmare. articles.title: Mistress may have handed prosecutors missing ‘why’ in ‘American Idol’ alum’s wife murder case: expert
articles.summary: The Caleb Flynn trial took a dramatic turn as mistress Alleigha Botner read explosive texts exchanged in the months before Ashley Flynn's fatal shooting.
articles.body: The explosive testimony of Caleb Flynn's former mistress may have handed Ohio prosecutors a critical piece of their murder case against the former "American Idol" contestant – a potential answer to why he would allegedly kill his wife, a former prosecutor told Fox News Digital. "Motive. She provides a motive," Josh Ritter, a former prosecutor, criminal defense attorney and Fox News contributor, said of Alleigha Botner's testimony. "She gives jurors a reason for why would this man murder his wife." "She seems like she was, by all accounts, a very nice woman," Ritter said about Ashley Flynn. "She's the mother of his children. Yes, he wanted out of the marriage." "Perhaps there was some financial gain in the idea of life insurance, but, you know, jurors oftentimes struggle with that question," he added. DAD OF 'AMERICAN IDOL' CONTESTANT'S SLAIN WIFE MADE EERIE GOOGLE SEARCH AFTER HEARING OF HER MURDER Flynn is accused of fatally shooting his wife in the back of the head inside their Ohio home on Feb. 16 and staging the scene to look like an intruder had broken in. He has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder and other charges. Botner, who testified she carried on an affair with Flynn for roughly a year and a half, spent two days walking jurors through many of the 107,000-plus messages exchanged during their relationship. NEW JERSEY MAN ACCUSED OF KILLING WIFE WITH BARBELL ALLEGEDLY CONFESSED IN MESSAGES TO RELATIVES: REPORT Some contained explicit discussions about Ashley's death. In one May 2025 message, Flynn allegedly wrote, "If I could literally kill her and not go to hell, I would do it in a heartbeat." RUSSIAN SPIES ORCHESTRATED $40K MURDER PLOT IN NATION’S CAPITAL, US ALLEGES Days later, he allegedly wrote, "I hate her, loathe her. I want her dead." In June, Flynn allegedly told Botner, "Please hire someone to take [her] out. I need you in my life, I need you." SCOTT PETERSON'S DEFENSE LOSES BID TO INTRODUCE WITNESS TESTIMONY IN LONG-RUNNING FIGHT TO OVERTURN CONVICTION Botner responded, "So tempting. I can't live without you. And I've had this thought so often lately. How do we figure this out?" Botner also became emotional while reading one of her own messages to Flynn, expressing regrets that she wished she never wrote it. ALEX MURDAUGH LAWYERS ALLEGE ‘FABRICATED’ EVIDENCE WAS USED TO SECURE MURDER INDICTMENTS "I want to kill her, Caleb," she had written. "That makes two of us," Flynn allegedly responded. ALEX MURDAUGH MAKES 'EXPLOSIVE' BID TO BLOW UP MURDER CASE HINGING ON DNA, DIRTY MONEY AND LIES: EXPERT Ritter said it is the substance of those exchanges – rather than simply the existence of the affair or sheer volume of messages – that could prove significant for prosecutors. "It's the idea that he's even discussing her being dead," Ritter said. "He went as far as to saying I literally would kill her. That's far beyond someone voicing their frustrations and venting to a lover that I wish my wife wasn't around, I wish she would leave, I wish we could get a divorce." "This is saying you want that person dead, that, in your view, that is your solution to the problem that you have," he added. The messages grew particularly significant as prosecutors moved jurors closer to the night Ashley was killed. FLORIDA PLASTIC SURGEON FOUND GUILTY OF MURDERING ATTORNEY WHO VANISHED FROM BLOODY OFFICE Botner testified that Flynn told her in an August message he had stayed up until 4 a.m. "literally thinking of ways to kill her and not go to jail." Months later, Botner gave Flynn a Jan. 11 ultimatum to leave Ashley or she would end their relationship. When he failed to do so, Botner cut off communication until Feb. 14 – just two days before Ashley's death. By the night of Feb. 15, the two were communicating again. Botner testified that Flynn discussed his plans for the following day, including telling family members about the divorce and obtaining a burner phone. Shortly after midnight, Flynn allegedly wrote to Botner, "It's happening." He then wrote, "February 16th – day I'll never forget." "You're about to be free," Botner responded. "I choose you," Flynn replied. Those were some of the final messages Flynn sent Botner before she learned Ashley had been killed, she testified. Ritter pointed to that timing as among the most significant evidence Botner brought to the prosecution's case. He noted that Flynn had spent months allegedly talking about wanting Ashley dead before the messages reached the eve of her killing. "The day before the murder takes place, he tells his mistress that tomorrow is going to be a big day, that he chooses her," Ritter explained. "He's made a decision and that tomorrow, meaning February 16th, the date his wife was murdered, will be a day that he will never forget." But Ritter said the same enormous volume of messages prosecutors are using against Flynn also gives his attorneys an argument. The defense can contend prosecutors have cherry-picked the most damaging statements from more than 100,000 messages exchanged during an intense affair and stripped them of the broader context of two people using exaggerated and sometimes ugly language. Flynn's attorneys can also argue that when he talked about what would happen Feb. 16, he was referring to finally leaving Ashley – not killing her. WATCH: Caleb Flynn had ominous response when mistress said ‘I want to kill her’ "That could be true," Ritter said. "It could be that he is just the unluckiest man on earth, that the day he tells his mistress he's going to announce to his wife that he's leaving her after months of saying that he wants her dead, that some random home burglar happens to break in with no signs of forced entry, goes to his vehicle, knows exactly where to find his handgun, marches upstairs, puts two bullets in the back of his wife's head while she's sleeping, and leaves the rest of the house undisturbed." During cross-examination Thursday, Flynn's attorneys began putting Botner's own language before the jury. FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X "I'm so done with you. You have murdered my heart," Botner acknowledged writing Flynn during one argument. "I hope you're glad you took my virginity and also my heart and stomped all over it. Enjoy your marriage. I'm done." The defense also has another potentially important distinction to emphasize, Ritter said. Despite Flynn's repeated statements about wanting Ashley dead, he never explicitly told Botner he intended to carry out her killing. "There was never an explicit mention of, 'I'm going to do it, I'm gonna follow through on it,'" Ritter said. SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS "I think they are also going to concentrate on the idea, as they have since opening statements, that this might have been a rush to judgment, that once police uncovered the affair, they stopped their investigation," Ritter said. "And once they knew that he was planning on leaving his wife, they thought, 'Well, that's enough for us. We're not going to pursue other leads.'" CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB "I'm not saying that's a convincing argument, but I'm saying that that is at least something for them to stand on and mount a defense on his behalf," he added. WATCH: Caleb Flynn mistress drops bombshells in dramatic testimony SEND US A TIP The defense can also point to the absence of the alleged murder weapon, an eyewitness to the shooting and gunshot residue on Flynn. GOT A TIP? Botner testified, however, that Flynn had previously shown her a gun he kept inside the center console of his truck, though she could not remember what it looked like. LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST "In an ideal world, would the prosecution want the murder weapon? Sure," Ritter said. "But ... it's something that the defense is obviously going to lean into." GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL But for Ritter, Botner's testimony ultimately comes back to the question prosecutors hope jurors will ask when they consider the killing – why? articles.title: Pezeshkian says Iran ‘no longer trusts talks with Washington’
articles.summary: In an interview with Al Jazeera, the Iranian president says Qatar and Pakistan are relaying Tehran’s messages to the US.
articles.body:
President Masoud Pezeshkian has told Al Jazeera that Iran no longer trusts negotiations with the United States after previous rounds of talks were followed by attacks and sanctions, as Tehran awaits a response to its latest proposal to end the war.

“We have no trust in the American side and do not know on what basis an understanding can be reached with it,” Pezeshkian told the Qatar-based broadcaster in an interview aired on Saturday.

Pezeshkian and Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi visited the US this week for the United Nations gathering of world leaders and proposed a deal that would end fighting in the US-Israel war on Iran and unblock the Strait of Hormuz within seven days.

Araghchi told reporters on Friday that initial steps would take four to five days, the Strait of Hormuz would reopen on the sixth day and “on day seven, the talks with the US will be started for the final deal on mutually agreed subjects,” referring to Iran’s nuclear programme.

Under the plan, Washington would lift its naval blockade of Iranian ports, waive sanctions on Iranian oil sales, release an estimated $12bn in frozen Iranian assets and observe a ceasefire covering the region, including Lebanon and Yemen.

In return, Iran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world’s traded oil and gas passed before the war, and which has become Tehran’s main point of leverage.

Pezeshkian told Al Jazeera that mediators Qatar and Pakistan are conveying Iran’s messages to Washington. He said the negotiations are based on the previous memorandum of understanding (MoU) reached by the two sides in June, and the US must clarify its position on that agreement, which lapsed last month.

The war began in late February, when the US and Israel launched attacks on Iran that killed Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

Pezeshkian also denied that Iran was responsible for blocking the Strait of Hormuz, saying the US “closed the routes before us”. He described the closure as “a natural response when routes are cut off to Iran”.

He said the crisis could be resolved through negotiations rather than force, and that the waterway would reopen to commercial shipping if talks ended the war.

Pezeshkian called the US the aggressor in the conflict, saying Iran “has not attacked any country in 200 years”. He said the US and Israel had dragged regional countries into the war in the belief that the Iranian system “would collapse within days”.

“We withstood the American and Israeli attacks, and we will continue to stand firm,” he said, adding that neither the killing of an Iranian commander nor economic pressure had caused Iranians to retreat.

He said Israel and the US had attacked Iran from the airspace of Islamic countries, and that Iran targets bases used by US forces in the region because operations against it are launched from them. Tehran seeks nothing outside international law, he said, and responds only when others violate the rules.

Pezeshkian also linked the imposition of sanctions on Iran to the tactics used by Israel in its genocidal war against Palestinians in Gaza.

“Those who deny Iranians medicine and raw materials are the same people who cut off food and water from Gaza,” he said, adding that anyone who believed Iranians could be targeted through sanctions had “miscalculated”.

Pezeshkian also said regional security could be achieved through cooperation among the region’s own countries. “We do not need a regional policeman,” he said.

He accused the US and Israel of seeking to pit Islamic countries against one another to control the region’s resources. He also said Saudi Arabia is capable of playing a role in uniting the Islamic world.

Regarding Yemen, where fighting has escalated between the Iran-aligned Houthi rebels and Yemen’s Saudi-backed government forces, he said the actions of the Houthis were not connected to Iran, and that Tehran stands in solidarity with “everyone subjected to injustice”.

He urged the Houthis and Saudi Arabia to resolve their differences through dialogue, saying “a brother should not fight his brother,” and offered Iran’s help in ending the dispute. “We will not be warmongers,” he said.

On domestic politics, Pezeshkian accused Iran’s “enemies” of trying to stir disagreements among Iranian officials, insisting the country is witnessing “unprecedented unity and cohesion”.

He said he had met twice with Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, who has not appeared in public since the war began, including one meeting that lasted seven hours and covered pivotal issues. He pledged to overcome what he called “accumulated imbalances in Iran’s internal conditions”.

The US and Israel want to stop Iran from becoming self-reliant, he said, “but we will invest in our people”.

articles.title: Cornwall's Carn to Cove celebrates 25 years of rural arts touring
articles.summary: The rural touring arts scheme has brought performances to communities for more than two decades.
articles.body:
A touring arts scheme has marked 25 years of bringing music and theatre to rural areas of Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly.

Creative Kernow's rural touring scheme, Carn to Cove, marked the milestone at an event at Perranporth Memorial Hall on Friday, joined by founders, promoters, performers and rural touring leaders.

Founder and former Creative Kernow director, Ross Williams, said he was "really proud" of the scheme's quarter-century success.

Culture and place manager at Creative Kernow, Louise Kemp, said the anniversary was "so special", adding "I'm just so grateful that we can keep going after 25 years."

The programme works with village halls and community venues to bring professional performances, such as dance, theatre, comedy and music to audiences.

It has reached about 4,500 audience members since it was founded and worked with more than 2,300 artists.

For Kemp, the anniversary was a chance to celebrate both longevity and ambition.

She said: "We're working with more and more promoters across Cornwall so we can get to every neighbourhood, hopefully.

"It's really important to us that everyone gets to see something that might appeal to them."

The foundations for Carn to Cove were laid at the turn of the millennium.

Williams, who was the chief executive of Creative Kernow for 30 years, said the late 1990s and early 2000s were a particularly positive period for arts funding.

"There was more money around, and the Arts Council was keen to support county-wide schemes," he said.

Working with Cornwall Council and arts officer Jennifer Lowe, organisers developed a pilot project before securing funding for a county wide scheme.

Williams said performers would often stay with local people in a bid to keep costs down.

"That's just really fascinating," he said. "I think we've had people from all over the world staying with us in our cottage in Stithians," he said.

"They're natural storytellers, all these people. So, it's very easy to get on with them and I think that's a really warm sort of human part of the scheme.

"I just think it's an amazing way of introducing the world to Cornwall and Cornwall to the world, because you get such a choice of people."

Former scheme manager Claire Marshall dedicated about 17 years to Carn to Cove.

"Quite a large part of my life was given over to rural touring," she said.

"Carn to Cove was used as a model or a mentor for several countries in Europe who wanted to set up their own schemes.

"So I guess that's the thing that sort of sticks with me the most."

Marshall also highlighted the opportunities the scheme creates for local performers, including aspiring actors who look to move out of Cornwall.

"They don't need to," she said. "Rural touring is an actual job. It's a route into theatre-making and music."

Now working as a promoter herself, Marshall still has ties with the scheme which puts on events at the venues she works and volunteers with.

"Carn to Cove will always be with me, I think," she said.
